 6 Ideal Destinations For A Passport-Free 3-Day Weekend From The U.S.

 By  
 Becca Billis 
 Published Nov 20, 2026, 10:16 PM EST 
 Becca is a British travel writer and editor based in Mexico City who specializes in Mexico stories. Her love for travel began as a teenager on a solo Interrail trip around Italy, where she realized that travel was the perfect intersection of learning, eating, and meeting new people. That adventure kickstarted her career in travel media, starting at a sustainability-focused PR and marketing agency and later leading to a master’s degree in journalism with a focus on travel writing. Since then, her work has ranged from writing for national tourism boards to sharing advice for mindful yet budget-friendly trips.
She is always looking for new destinations, especially places where she can try the local cuisine, scuba dive, and dig into cultural practices and history. When she is not writing or editing, she can usually be found eating her way across Mexico City with her partner or planning their next adventure.

 With the holiday season upon us, many American travelers are looking to get their next long weekend away booked. Whether it is a few days relaxing on tropical Caribbean beaches or heading north to chase whales and waterfalls in Canada, there are plenty of options for a stress-free, passport-free, three-day break from the U.S.

 Renewing or ordering a passport can be an expensive and lengthy process. In November 2026, new rules were introduced that let certain adults apply for their first passport online without visiting a passport facility. Although this makes things slightly easier, the $130 application fee for an adult passport book still applies. ID regulations have also started to change; TSA introduced new rules for U.S. travelers as REAL ID enforcement nears , including new travel requirements for both domestic and international flights. 
 So where exactly can Americans get that international feeling without a passport? From flying to U.S. territories such as Puerto Rico to setting sail on a closed-loop international cruise or crossing into Canada, here are six long-weekend ideas, including what travelers can expect and which ID they should pack.

 By  
 Justin Fenwick 
 San Juan, Puerto Rico
 A street view of San Juan, Puerto Rico's capital and largest city Credit: Shutterstock 
 The Puerto Rican capital was colonized by Spain more than 500 years ago and came under U.S. control in 1898, making it culturally Latin while still part of the United States. Visitors can expect to find endless restaurants serving up everything from the Caribbean to Chinese dishes. Start the day by exploring colonial landmarks such as the fortress Castillo San Felipe del Morro, then salsa the evening away with live music in one of the city's buzzing bars.
 Head to Viejo San Juan, otherwise known as Old San Juan, for colorful buildings lining cobbled streets inside centuries-old city walls. When it's time for a sun and sea fix, the white-sand shores of Isla Verde Beach are about a 15-minute drive from Old San Juan, while Condado Beach sits a stone’s throw from the city center.
 Condado Beach in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Caribbean Credit: Shutterstock 
 Nonstop flights take about 2 hours 45 minutes from Miami and 3.5 to 4 hours from hubs such as New York and Atlanta. The average daily cost sits around $243, according to Budget Your Trip, nearly $100 a day less than the U.S. average, which ranked as the most expensive country for travelers in 2026 . Excluding flights, travelers can expect to spend around $729 per person over three days. Logistics are simple, too: U.S. phone plans work, and the island's currency is the U.S. dollar.
 Because Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, there's no passport check or customs on arrival from the mainland. Travelers do still need a REAL ID-compliant license or other TSA-accepted ID to fly there and back. Anyone without one will need to pay the $45 ConfirmID fee, which still doesn’t guarantee they’ll clear security.
 St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands
 Blue waters and lush hillsides on the St. Croix coastline in the U.S. Virgin Islands Credit: Shutterstock 
 The largest of the U.S. Virgin Islands feels worlds away from the continental U.S., with thick tropical rainforest, crystal-blue waters and mangrove-knotted shorelines. Travelers can spend a weekend hiking coastal trails or snorkeling the coral reefs at Buck Island Reef National Monument. Alternatively, head to Christiansted and Frederiksted to learn about the island’s colonial history at sites such as Fort Christiansvaern, or retrace the footsteps of a young Alexander Hamilton, who worked as a clerk in Christiansted. Don’t leave without a taste of fish and fungi or a slice of rum-drenched black cake.
 Nonstop flights take about 2 hours 40 minutes from Miami and around 3.5 hours from Atlanta and Charlotte. U.S. citizens arriving from the mainland don’t need a passport, according to the USVI Department of Tourism , but travelers 18 and older do need a REAL ID-compliant license or other TSA-accepted ID at airport security. The USVI Department of Tourism told TheTravel that St. Croix welcomed 152,906 of the territory’s 770,422 visitor arrivals from January through October 2026.
 The USVI Department of Tourism told TheTravel that visitors must be ready to show proof of citizenship when departing the territory, such as a raised-seal birth certificate with a government-issued photo ID, though the department highlighted that a valid U.S. passport remains the preferred document.
 “From the historic charm of Christiansted and the pristine waters of Buck Island to our vibrant culinary scene and rich cultural traditions, St. Croix offers visitors an authentic Caribbean experience that is uniquely its own,” Jennifer Matarangas-King, Commissioner of Tourism for the U.S. Virgin Islands told TheTravel.
 The passport exemption also doesn’t extend to the nearby British Virgin Islands, a separate British Overseas Territory, so anyone planning a day trip there will need a passport.
 Bahamas Closed-Loop Cruise From Miami
 2 Carnival cruise ships docked at Celebration Key, East Grand Bahama, The Bahamas Credit: Carnival Newsroom 
 For travelers who want to eliminate the travel stress entirely, a closed-loop cruise to the Bahamas is one of the simplest options. Carnival Conquest, home ported year-round in Miami, sails three-night weekend voyages that leave on Friday afternoons and return Monday mornings. Alongside a day at sea enjoying the ship's onboard activities, guests disembark at Celebration Key, Carnival's beach destination on Grand Bahama Island, for a day of white sand and turquoise water.
 U.S. Customs and Border Protection states that under the Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative , U.S. citizens on a closed-loop cruise , one that begins and ends at the same U.S. port, can sail with a government-issued photo ID plus an original or certified birth certificate instead of a passport. Children under 16 can use their birth certificate alone.
 A REAL ID on its own won't get travelers on board, because it proves identity, not citizenship. CBP also warns that countries on the route can still require a passport, and Carnival encourages guests to bring one anyway because anyone who misses the ship in port or needs to fly home early from the Bahamas will need a passport to board a flight back to the U.S.
 Ensenada Closed-Loop Cruise From Southern California
 Aerial Photo of the Navigator of the Seas Credit: Royal Caribbean Press Center 
 It isn't just Florida that offers passport-free cruise routes; West Coast travelers can head south on a short closed-loop cruise from the Los Angeles area to Ensenada, Mexico. The port city is located in Mexico's Baja California, loved for its cacti-studded desert landscape, fish tacos, and the dramatic La Bufadora geyser. Royal Caribbean's Navigator of the Seas runs a three-night package from $467 USD per person.
 The same CBP rule applies as in the Bahamas: a government-issued photo ID plus an original or certified birth certificate, or the birth certificate alone for children under 16. However, just like in the Bahamas, a port on the route can still ask for a passport, and anyone who misses the ship or decides to fly home from Mexico will need one.
 Victoria, British Columbia, Canada
 Victoria Inner Harbour view with British Columbia Parliament and flowers Credit: Diego Grandi / Shutterstock.com 
 Perched on the southern tip of Vancouver Island, Victoria is loved for its mild climate and endless green open spaces. It suits travelers who want a weekend of everything from exploring the Royal BC Museum to tucking into a British-style afternoon tea or boarding a boat to spot whales and other local wildlife.
 The city sits just across the water from Washington state and is reached by ferry. Black Ball Ferry Line's M.V. Coho runs from Port Angeles in about 90 minutes, carrying both walk-on passengers and vehicles. The Victoria Clipper , a passenger-only catamaran, links downtown Seattle and Victoria in roughly 2 hours 45 minutes. Both dock in the Inner Harbour, a short walk from the Fairmont Empress and the Royal BC Museum.
 Enhanced Driver's Licenses: An EDL is a state driver's license that also proves U.S. citizenship. Only five states issue them: Michigan, Minnesota, New York, Vermont, and Washington. According to CBP, EDLs work for land and sea border crossings, but not for international flights.
 Both ferries accept a valid passport, a U.S. passport card, a NEXUS card, or an EDL. A REAL ID won't be accepted, as both operators state it isn't valid for an international border crossing. As for pricing, Budget Your Trip estimated the average daily cost at around $215, or about $645 per person for three days, excluding the ferry.
 Niagara Falls, Ontario, Canada
 Canadian side view of Niagara Falls, Horseshoe Falls and boat tour at sunset in Niagara Falls, Ontario, Canada Credit: Shutterstock 
 Niagara Falls, Ontario, offers the view most visitors come for, looking across at the American Falls towards Horseshoe Falls. The Rainbow Bridge, open 24 hours a day, links Niagara Falls, New York, to the Canadian side and is the closest crossing to the falls and Clifton Hill, which can be explored on foot.
 After sightseeing, travelers can unwind with a day wandering Niagara-on-the-Lake’s Queen Street boutiques and sampling local wines grown and produced from nearby vineyards, all of which is only about a 20-minute drive north along the Niagara Parkway. The falls are about 30 minutes from Buffalo and roughly four hours from Detroit.
 This trip suits residents of the five EDL states, though anyone with a passport card can make it, too. Canada requires U.S. citizens to show proof of citizenship and identity, and to get back into the U.S. by land, travelers 16 and older need a passport, passport card, NEXUS card, or EDL. It's important to note that a birth certificate and driver's license won't get adults back into the U.S., and neither will a REAL ID. Budget Your Trip puts the average daily cost at around $205, or about $615 per person for three days, excluding gas.

 For travelers who take regular land or sea trips but don't live in an EDL state, a passport card can fill the gap. A first adult card costs $30 plus the $35 acceptance fee, compared with $130 for a passport book, according to the State Department . It works for land and sea travel to Canada, Mexico, Bermuda and the Caribbean, but not for international flights.
 The card is also an accepted ID at TSA checkpoints, so it covers every trip on this list. For anyone who might fly abroad, though, the book remains the more flexible choice, and first-time applicants can order both together for $160 plus the acceptance fee.
